groups.etymology: Inherited from Old French cail, specifically from forms without the final l such as kay, kai. Doublet of age and haie.

ex.fr: Il a toutes les qualités d'un bon président.
ex.en: He has all the qualities of a good president.

groups.etymology: From Old French, from Latin qualitātem.

ex.fr: Le Gros-Caillou est l'un des quartiers les plus riches de Paris.
ex.en: Gros-Caillou is one of the richest neighborhoods in Paris.

senses.d: piece, chunk; segment (of fruit), quarter (of beef)

groups.etymology: From quart + -ier, possibly Medieval Latin quarterium, compare also Latin quartārium; cognate with Italian quartiere.
Inherited from Old French quelesquunques, a borrowing of Latin qualiscumque, matched to the Old French quel (“which”) + que (“what”) + onques (“ever”). See Italian qualunque, a similar formation.
Inherited from Middle French quelquefoys, equivalent to quelque (“some”) + fois (“time”). Compare Walloon kécfeye.
Inherited from Middle French queu, cueue, from Old French cue, coe, from Vulgar Latin cōda, variant of Latin cauda. Doublet of coda.

c'est le serpent qui se mord la queue
ne pas avoir mis la queue aux cerises

senses.d: to part with somebody, to leave somebody

groups.etymology: From quitte + -er, or from Late Latin quietare (“acquit, discharge, release”), from Latin quiētāre (“to calm”).
Learned borrowing from Latin quotīdiānus, late spelling of Classical cottīdiānus, from cottīdiē (“daily”); cognate with English quotidian.

senses.d: a daily, a daily paper: a newspaper that is published daily
